say: What does a nine rupee store cost? Swiggy's letter to shareholders lists it among the price offers it ran on Instamart, its quick delivery app.

The letter gives no price for it. It does give Instamart's loss: eight hundred and ninety five crore last quarter, on the company's own measure, adjusted EBITDA. The quarter before: seven hundred and seventy eight.

Now the other half. On that measure, Swiggy's food delivery made a record three hundred and forty one crore. On Instamart, the letter says: 'we chose to calibrate near-term investments to accelerate growth'.
So our question: what is that loss buying, and what does Swiggy say it needs before the losses stop?

First, the part with a profit on the company's own measure. Food orders came to ten thousand and fifty four crore rupees, counted before discounts: seventeen point seven percent more than a year earlier.
Out of every hundred rupees of food orders, about three rupees forty was left as adjusted EBITDA, the company's own measure. A year earlier, the letter's chart shows two rupees eighty.
Why did it rise? Some of the levers, the letter says. First, advertising, which lifted Swiggy's cut of each food order, its take rate, to twenty six point one percent, its highest ever.

Second, delivery cost efficiency, from orders that sit closer together and shorter trips. The letter ties that to Bolt and the ninety nine store, together more than a quarter of food delivery volumes.

So is the whole company in profit? No. Group revenue rose to seven thousand five hundred and seventy one crore, up thirty six percent by our arithmetic. Yet on the standard accounts, unaudited, the group lost nine hundred and twenty two crore: less than a year earlier, more than the quarter before.

So, what did the loss buy? Instamart delivers groceries and household items from small warehouses it calls dark stores. Last quarter, the value of its orders, after discounts, grew thirteen point four percent in just three months.

In the two quarters before, that growth was four percent and two and a half. So it sped up. Instamart's average monthly ordering users grew by one point three million, its most in five quarters, to fourteen point eight million.
Did users stay? The letter says month-one retention averaged over sixty percent, meaningfully higher than in earlier quarters. It does not define the term.

Sixty nine net new dark stores in one quarter, as many as the three quarters before combined, for one thousand two hundred and forty in all. Each store got busier: one thousand one hundred and ninety two orders a day, up from one thousand and eighty nine.

So what did it cost? Swiggy's cut of each Instamart order fell one point four percentage points in a quarter. After the direct costs of orders, called contribution, Instamart broke even in May, the letter says. For the quarter it was minus one percent of gross order value, inside the company's guided range.

The letter splits that quarter's fall in contribution. One percentage point went on what it calls 'Targeted investments' in habit formation and winning back dormant users. Our reading: that is where offers like the nine rupee store sit.
Another zero point four points came from a changing mix of users and categories. Cost efficiencies, mainly busier stores, clawed back zero point six. Net fall: zero point eight.

And the loss? Eight hundred and ninety five crore, one hundred and eighteen more than the quarter before. Here is the twist. As a share of gross order value, it barely moved: minus nine point eight to minus nine point seven percent. By our arithmetic, order value grew a little faster than the loss.

So when do the losses stop? Here is how far the letter goes: 'We believe the Adjusted EBITDA losses to have peaked out', it says, in the quarter just gone. It also expects the price offers to start reversing over the next couple of quarters.

For the December quarter, it expects Instamart's adjusted EBITDA margin to improve by about one point of gross order value. And it spells out what break-even on that measure needs. First, about two point three times today's size.
That means sixty thousand crore rupees of orders a year, after discounts, up from twenty six thousand four hundred crore today.
Second, thirty rupees of contribution per order. Today, by our arithmetic, at the quarter's average order of seven hundred and eight rupees, it is about minus seven rupees.
Where would that money come from? Roughly two thirds, the letter says, from earning more per order: product mix, own brands and advertising. One third from lower costs: density, automation and scale.

And a rule change. Shareholders approved capping foreign ownership at forty nine and a half percent, to qualify as Indian owned and controlled. That lets Instamart own the stock it sells, from the middle of the December quarter. Swiggy says it could add about zero point eight points to contribution.
But. Almost everything in that last chapter is the company's own forecast or target. And this letter gives no date for when Instamart breaks even.
On competition, in its words: 'Competitive intensity in the sector remains high, and we do not expect it to ease in the near-term'.

The letter also expects contribution to stay between zero and minus one percent in the December quarter, with improvement after that. At today's average order, that is zero to minus seven rupees, by our arithmetic, against the thirty it needs.

A rival is much larger. In Eternal's own letter of the twenty first of October, Blinkit's order value is about three times Instamart's, by our arithmetic, and its adjusted EBITDA, on its own measure, was a profit.

Meanwhile, the group's cash balance fell by about seven hundred crore in the quarter, to thirteen thousand six hundred and sixty two crore. And Toing, its budget meals app, sits inside a unit called Platform Innovations.

That unit's loss, on the company's measure, rose to one hundred and sixty two crore, from forty six a year earlier. The letter does not say how much of that is Toing. It expects Toing's overall investment to stay range bound for now.

Swiggy calls its price offers 'discretionary and transient'. Our reading: a choice can be reversed, but with competition not expected to ease, the company may not be the only one deciding how long the spending lasts.
So, back to the nine rupee store. By our arithmetic, the average Instamart order ended the quarter about seven rupees short after its direct costs. Swiggy says it needs thirty rupees left over.
The first checkpoint is the December quarter, when Swiggy expects Instamart's margin to improve by about one point. Its next letter will show whether the loss fell.
